overview: The Abdelwadids, also called Zayyanids, made Tlemcen the capital of a kingdom in the central Maghreb. Emerging from Zenata leadership as Almohad power weakened, they supported a city connected to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade.

periods.title: An independent court at Tlemcen
periods.summary: Yaghmurasan took power in 1236 and asserted independence from the Almohads. Tlemcen became the centre of his dynasty.

periods.title: The long siege
periods.summary: A Marinid siege began in 1299, placing Tlemcen under prolonged military pressure.

periods.title: Recovery and royal building
periods.summary: The siege ended in 1307. Under Abu Hammu I and Abu Tashfin, the kingdom recovered and expanded its authority.

periods.title: Marinid conquest and contested rule
periods.summary: The Marinid ruler Abu al-Hasan captured Tlemcen in 1337. Subsequent occupations interrupted Zayyanid power without permanently eliminating the dynasty.

periods.title: A restored but contested kingdom
periods.summary: Abu Hammu II restored Zayyanid rule, although repeated foreign intervention and internal rivalries continued to constrain the kingdom.

periods.title: Loss of ports and independence
periods.summary: Spain’s occupation of Oran in 1509 deprived Tlemcen of a major port and customs income. Zayyanid rulers subsequently sought protection from competing Spanish and Ottoman powers.

sections.title: Markets and the people who made cloth

items.text: A marble tablet from Tlemcen’s bazaar carries an inscription dating it to 1328 and identifying it as a cubit measure. Its ruled line is divided into four parts. The object made a common unit of length physically available in a place of commerce.

The catalogue reports that this tablet was found set into the bazaar wall. It is evidence for a local measurement standard, not proof that the ruler invented the cubit or that every sale followed the rule without dispute.

Textile production employed both men and women in Zayyanid Tlemcen. A study of the industry links its growth to available raw materials, trading connections and expertise arriving from al-Andalus. Making cloth connected household livelihoods with the city’s wider economy.

The same study describes demand from different social groups, including elite customers seeking refined fabrics. Quality and finish mattered to makers as well as access to materials. The surviving record does not justify treating every textile worker as prosperous.

An inscription dates the Sidi Bel-Hasan mosque to 1296. Onyx columns support horseshoe arches dividing the prayer hall into three aisles, while cedar roof structures carried tile coverings. A relatively small building brought together stoneworking, carpentry and brick construction.

Traces of coloured paint survive on the mosque’s plaster decoration. Its prayer niche combines inscriptions and floral ornament with a muqarnas dome, formed from small projecting cells. Later alterations mean that the building’s present appearance is not wholly medieval.

At the royal Mechouar, Abu Hammu Musa I completed a mosque in 1317 to 1318. The square minaret preserves panels of small columns and arches against tiled mosaics. Its decoration records skilled work within the court’s architectural setting.

Tlemcen’s teaching took place in mosques and madrasas, with study of Islamic law, Qur’anic interpretation, hadith and Sufism. Rulers’ support helped attract teachers and students from other regions, connecting the city with a wider scholarly world.

The Mechouar began as Yaghmurasan’s royal seat in the thirteenth century and was enlarged by successors. Modern conservation has also shaped it: a project sheet records major work on tile and plaster decoration between 2008 and 2012. Present surfaces need to be read alongside that restoration history.

Two gold dinars in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, catalogued as Lavoix 986 and 987, name Tlemcen and two rulers. Mohamed Elhadri argues that they belong to sixteenth-century Zayyanids acknowledging the Ottoman sultan Süleyman, rather than an earlier Marinid and Nasrid alliance.

Elhadri tests that attribution against the names, titles and mint formulas on the coins and the chronology of political alliances. The case shows why a familiar royal name alone may misdate an object, especially when local monetary forms survive changes of overlord.

In 1517, one Tlemcen faction invited Aruj from Algiers while another backed the Zayyanid ruler with Spanish help. Aruj was killed after fleeing in 1518. Local choices and rivalries were central to this struggle, alongside the ambitions of larger powers.

ending.text: Ottoman expansion ended Zayyanid rule around the middle of the sixteenth century. Sources date the final transition differently; approximately 1554 is a conventional endpoint. The royal citadel passed into Ottoman use, while Tlemcen and its inhabitants continued beyond the dynasty.
